section.title: Hannah's Prayer
section.sectionRationale: Hannah's answered prayer overflows into a song, and the song sounds the keynote of the whole book. She does not merely thank God for a baby; she praises the God who reverses the world, breaking the bows of the mighty and lifting the poor from the dust. The song rises to a startling climax about a king and an anointed one who do not yet exist, so that a private thanksgiving becomes a prophecy of the kingdom to come. It is one movement: the theology of the entire book, sung.
section.thesis: The God who opened one barren womb is the God who topples the proud and exalts the humble, who kills and makes alive, and who will judge the earth and exalt the horn of His anointed King, so that Hannah's small deliverance becomes a window onto God's great reversal and the coming of His Messiah.
section.frameNote: Three movements of the song: praise for the God of reversal, verses 1 to 3; the great reversals He works, verses 4 to 8; and the LORD who judges the earth and exalts His anointed King, verses 9 to 10, with Samuel left ministering, verse 11.

units.label: Praise for the God of reversal
units.note: there is no Rock like our God

verses.text: At that time Hannah prayed: “My heart rejoices in the LORD; my {{qeren|horn}} is exalted in the LORD. My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies, for I rejoice in Your salvation.
There is no one holy like the LORD. Indeed, there is no one besides You! And there is no {{tsur|Rock}} like our God.
Do not boast so proudly, or let arrogance come from your mouth, for the LORD is a God who knows, and by Him actions are weighed.
The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble are equipped with strength.
The well-fed hire themselves out for food, but the starving hunger no more. The barren woman gives birth to seven, but she who has many sons pines away.
The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up.
The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts.

He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor. For the foundations of the earth are the LORD’s, and upon them He has set the world.

units.label: The LORD judges the earth and exalts His anointed
units.note: He will exalt the horn of His anointed

verses.text: He guards the steps of His faithful ones, but the wicked perish in darkness; for by his own strength shall no man prevail.

Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered. He will thunder from heaven against them. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth and will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His {{mashiach|anointed}}.”
Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest.

qeren.gloss: Horn. Drawn from the horn of a strong animal, it is a vivid image of strength, dignity, and victory. Hannah says her horn is exalted, her strength lifted up by the LORD; the song ends with God exalting the horn of His anointed. The word frames the whole prayer, from one woman's rescue to the strength of the coming King.

tsur.gloss: Rock. A favorite Old Testament name for God, picturing Him as unshakable refuge and sure foundation, Deuteronomy 32. Against a world of shifting fortunes and toppling powers, Hannah confesses there is no Rock like our God, the one steady ground beneath every reversal she sings.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one, messiah. The one set apart and empowered by God, marked out by anointing oil. Here, before Israel has any king, Hannah prophesies that God will exalt the horn of His anointed. It is the first sounding of a note that will swell through David to the true Messiah, Jesus Christ, the Anointed King.

basic.context: Once God answers her prayer and gives her Samuel, Hannah breaks into a song. But she does not simply celebrate her baby; she sings about the kind of God who gave him. He is the God who turns the world upside down: He breaks the strong and strengthens the weak, empties the full and fills the hungry, brings low and lifts up. At the very end she sings about a king and an anointed one, even though Israel has no king yet, so her thanksgiving becomes a prophecy. The big question the song answers is: what is God like? He is the God who lifts the lowly and will one day exalt His Messiah.
basic.hermeneutics: This is poetry, a song of praise, and it uses vivid images to make its point, bows broken, the hungry filled, the barren bearing seven. We should read it as worship and as prophecy, not as a flat promise that every faithful person will grow rich or have many children. Its enduring truth is who God is, the God of the great reversal, and its climax looks beyond Hannah's day to the King God will anoint.
basic.originalLanguages: Hannah sings that her qeren, her horn, her strength, is exalted, and that there is no tsur, no Rock, like our God, the one steady foundation under a shifting world. The song rises to the mashiach, the anointed one, God's King, a word used here before any king exists. From one woman's rescue the song reaches to the coming Messiah.
basic.typology: Hannah's song is the pattern for Mary's Magnificat; both women sing of a God who scatters the proud and lifts the humble, on the eve of a God-given son. The line about God bringing down to the grave and raising up foreshadows the death and resurrection at the heart of the gospel. And the anointed King she sings of points past David to Christ, the true Anointed One.
basic.christ: The song ends not with Hannah but with the LORD's anointed, His mashiach, His King. Israel had no king when she sang, so this is prophecy: God will raise up an anointed one and exalt his horn. That hope runs through David to Jesus, the Christ, the true and final Anointed King, who was brought down to the grave and raised up, and who is exalted to judge the ends of the earth. Hannah's small reversal is a signpost to the great reversal accomplished in Him.
basic.god: The God of this song is holy, unique, and unrivaled, the Rock. He knows all things and weighs every action, so no proud boast escapes Him. He is utterly sovereign over life and death, wealth and poverty, honor and shame. And He uses that total sovereignty to a moral end: to humble the proud and exalt the lowly, and finally to establish His anointed King.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 1 gives Mary's Magnificat, modeled on this song. Psalm 113 sings the same reversal, raising the poor from the dust. Matthew 5 blesses the poor in spirit and the hungry. And Philippians 2 shows Christ humbled to death and then highly exalted, the great reversal in person.
basic.oneStory: Hannah's thanksgiving becomes the theme song of 1 Samuel and of Scripture itself: God brings down the proud and lifts up the lowly. Her closing words about the anointed King reach past David to Christ. What God did in one barren womb He is doing in the whole story, running toward the Messiah whose horn He exalts forever.

context.literary: Hannah's song is the first of several poems Scripture sets like a hinge inside prose narrative, the technique of Exodus 15, Judges 5, and later 2 Samuel 22 and Luke 1. Each time, a character's personal deliverance becomes the occasion for a hymn that reads the whole story theologically rather than merely reporting it. The prayer itself moves in three unequal steps that mirror each other: verses 1 to 3 open with Hannah's own mouth, boasting in the LORD rather than against her rivals; verses 4 to 8 pile up six paired reversals in tight parallel lines, each clause answered by its opposite, bows broken against the feeble armed, the full selling their labor against the hungry ceasing to hunger; and verses 9 to 10 turn from proverb-like observation to direct address, ending on the unnamed king and the anointed one. The horn that opens the song in verse 1 returns in its very last line, so the whole poem is framed by the same image, tying Hannah's own lifted horn to the horn of the coming king. Verse 11 drops back into plain prose with almost no ceremony, Elkanah simply goes home, which throws the height of the song into relief: an ordinary family's morning after is interrupted by a hymn that reaches to the ends of the earth. The Hebrew term for the anointed king in the song's last line will reappear as an inclusio at the very end of 2 Samuel, so that Hannah's private thanksgiving and the mature monarchy at the book's close answer one another across the whole double work.
context.historical: Thanksgiving songs like this one had a recognized shape in Israel's worship: a vow made in distress, Hannah's own vow of 1:11, was answered, and the worshiper returned to the sanctuary to sing publicly what God had done, much as many psalms of thanksgiving open with a rescue and move to praise before the assembled congregation. Shiloh, where Hannah stands, housed the ark and functioned as Israel's central sanctuary before Jerusalem existed, so her song was not a private lyric but liturgy spoken where all Israel gathered for the yearly sacrifices mentioned back in chapter 1. The horn that frames her song was a familiar image across the ancient Near East, drawn from the horned animals of sacrifice and from horned altars and headdresses that marked strength, dignity and often royal or divine power; an exalted horn signaled a status publicly restored, not merely private relief. Her language that the pillars of the earth belong to the LORD reflects the common ancient picture of a stable earth resting on foundations, an idiom used elsewhere in Job and the Psalms to affirm that the visible order itself answers to God rather than floating free of Him. Perhaps most striking for its first hearers, Israel in this period had no king at all; the book of Judges that stands just before Samuel ends by lamenting that everyone did what was right in his own eyes because there was no king. Into that very setting, a woman at a rural sanctuary sings of a king before Israel has ever had one, a note her earliest audience would have felt as strange and electric.
context.canonical: Hannah's rock language borrows directly from the closing hymn of the Torah: Deuteronomy 32:39, where Moses has the LORD declare, I bring death and I give life, gives Hannah words she echoes closely in verse 6, and Deuteronomy 32:4 and 32:31 already call the LORD the Rock beside whom there is no other. By singing in these terms, Hannah shows herself steeped in Israel's oldest liturgy, and the narrator quietly signals that her private prayer stands in an unbroken line with Moses' public song. Psalm 113 takes up her picture of the poor lifted from the dust and the ash heap almost word for word, and Psalm 75:10 later promises that God will cut off the horns of the wicked while lifting the horns of the righteous, extending the very image Hannah opens and closes with. The claim that no one is holy like the LORD anticipates the refrain of Isaiah's later prophecy, where God alone is called the Holy One of Israel again and again. Within Samuel itself, the horn and the anointed king that close her song return at the seam of the two books: David's own last words in 2 Samuel 22:32 pick up rock language nearly word for word, so that Hannah's opening hymn and David's closing psalm form bookends around the entire narrative of the rise of the monarchy. Later Scripture keeps returning to this song rather than letting it stand alone, which is itself a sign of how the canon received it, not as a private lyric but as programmatic praise.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The narrator places this song exactly here, not merely because Hannah happened to sing it, so that everything that follows will be read through it. Every reversal in 1 and 2 Samuel, the fall of Eli's proud house against the rise of the humble Samuel, later the collapse of Saul against the rise of the shepherd David, is meant to be heard as one more instance of what Hannah has already announced: the LORD humbles and the LORD exalts. The author also wants his readers to see prayer answered rightly: Hannah does not simply take her long-awaited son and go home quietly; she turns her personal rescue into public praise about who God is, teaching that the right response to answered prayer is theology, not merely relief. By ending on an unnamed king and anointed one while Israel has no king, the writer plants a seed of expectation at the very start of the book that will not be harvested until Samuel anoints Saul, and then David, teaching the first readers to hold their history loosely, watching for the king God Himself would raise up rather than the king they might otherwise demand for themselves.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Hannah's verses describe how God has acted and does act; they are doxology, not a checklist of guaranteed outcomes for anyone who prays hard enough. Verse 9, that no one prevails by his own strength, is a wisdom generalization in the same vein as Ecclesiastes and Proverbs, true as a rule about ultimate outcomes without promising that every strong person will fall today or that every weak believer is shielded from harm this week; Job's friends made exactly this mistake by treating poetic generalizations as ironclad formulas. Nor does the song prescribe poverty as inherently righteous or wealth as inherently wicked; it praises the God who sends both, verse 7, and who is free to reverse either. What does carry forward as binding teaching is the character disclosed here, that all human strength and standing are held on loan from a sovereign God who may withdraw or give them, and that boasting belongs to Him alone, never to what our own hand has secured.

debates.question: How can Hannah sing of the LORD's king and anointed when Israel has no king yet?

views.label: Genuine prophecy given by the Spirit
views.case: Hannah, or the Spirit speaking through her placed song, looks ahead to the monarchy God is about to raise up; the song functions as prophecy, setting the messianic hope at the very door of the book before any king exists.

views.label: The narrator's inspired framing of the whole book
views.case: The song is positioned by the author to interpret all that follows, anticipating Saul and David and reaching toward the anointed King; its royal climax is a deliberate literary and theological signpost, not an anachronism.

debates.bearing: Either way the closing line lifts the reader's eyes beyond Hannah's baby to the King God will anoint, a hope that runs through David to Christ, the true Messiah.

debates.question: Is the promised reversal material and immediate, or deeper and ultimate?

views.label: Real reversals in history
views.case: God truly does raise the poor and humble the mighty within history, as He did for Hannah and will do in toppling Eli's house and Saul's throne; the song celebrates God's actual dealings, not mere metaphor.

views.label: A pattern that reaches its fullness in the gospel
views.case: The reversals point beyond any single instance to God's ultimate work in Christ, who was brought low and raised up, and who blesses the poor in spirit; the deepest fulfillment is eschatological and messianic.

debates.bearing: Both are true and held together: God acts within history and points beyond it, so that Hannah's rescue and Christ's exaltation are of one piece, the same God working the same great reversal.

debates.question: Did Hannah compose this song for the occasion, or is it an older hymn placed fittingly on her lips?

views.label: A song composed for this occasion
views.case: The vocabulary fits her circumstance precisely, a barren womb reversed, personal exultation over one child, suggesting a fresh composition drawn directly from her own experience of answered prayer.

views.label: A communal hymn adapted to her story
views.case: The song's national and even monarchic scope, its king and anointed one sung before either existed, and its silence about Samuel, Elkanah, or Peninnah by name, suggest it may already have existed as temple thanksgiving liturgy that the narrator placed fittingly in her mouth.

debates.bearing: Either way Scripture presents the song as Hannah's own inspired words in the narrative, and its placement teaches that even the most personal answered prayer is meant to be voiced in the shared language of Israel's worship, not invented from nothing.

study.originalLanguages: Beyond the horn, the Rock and the anointed one that the lexicon already names, several other words carry weight in Hannah's Hebrew. In verse 3 she confesses that the LORD is El De'ot, literally a God of knowledges, the plural form intensifying rather than multiplying, a God whose knowing is total and by whom actions, the same word used of a set of scales, are weighed. Verse 4 names the fallen mighty as gibborim, the standard Old Testament term for warriors or heroes, so that broken bows belong to men whose very title means strength; their fall is not incidental weakness but the collapse of exactly those famed for might. Verse 5 turns on a pair of opposites, the sabim, the well fed or satisfied, who must now hire out their labor for bread, set against those once raevim, hungry, who hunger no more; the same verse names the aqarah, the barren woman, using the identical word Genesis uses of Sarah and Rachel, so that Hannah's own history joins a line of barren women through whom God works His purposes. Verse 6 is the theological hinge of the song: the LORD memit, brings to death, and mechayyeh, makes alive, sending down to Sheol and raising up. These verb forms echo Moses' own claim in Deuteronomy 32:39, I bring death and I give life, so Hannah is not inventing new theology but reciting the Torah's own confession about the God who alone holds the keys of death. Verse 8 piles up three words for the lowest of the low: the dal, the poor or thin one, is raised from the aphar, the dust, and the evyon, the needy, is lifted from the ashpoth, the ash heap or dunghill, the very place where the destitute were sometimes left to beg, so the imagery is not gentle poverty but the lowest social floor imaginable. That same verse claims that the metzukei aretz, the pillars or foundations of the earth, belong to the LORD, grounding the moral order of reversal in the physical order of creation itself; the world is not indifferent scaffolding but structure God Himself set and therefore structure that answers to His justice. Verse 9 calls the godly chasidav, His faithful or loyal ones, from the same root as chesed, covenant loyalty or steadfast love, so that those whose steps God guards are specifically those bound to Him in covenant love, not merely the morally upright in general. And the song's last line pairs melekh, king, with mashiach, anointed one, two words for the same coming figure, king by office and anointed by consecration, sung before either word had a living referent in Israel. Taken together, the vocabulary of this short song reaches back to Moses' Torah and forward to a king not yet born, binding the oldest confession of Israel's faith to the newest hope of its future.

typology.type: Hannah's song of the God who lifts the lowly
typology.fulfillment: Mary's Magnificat does not merely resemble Hannah's prayer, it reproduces its structure clause for clause: God has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts answers Hannah's broken bows of the mighty, and he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty answers Hannah's hungry ceasing to hunger while the well fed sell their labor. The escalation is the child each woman celebrates: Hannah's son is a prophet who will anoint a king, while Mary's son is the King Himself, so the pattern of praise for God's reversal reaches its true object only when a virgin, not merely a barren wife, becomes its unlikely vessel.

typology.type: The LORD who brings down to Sheol and raises up
typology.fulfillment: Hannah sings that the LORD brings down to Sheol and raises up, a general claim about God's sovereign power over every life and death in Israel's history. In the resurrection of Jesus that general truth becomes a single, unrepeatable event: God actually brought His own Son down to the grave and raised Him up on the third day, so that what Hannah confessed as a pattern across many lives becomes, in the gospel, one decisive act that secures resurrection for everyone joined to Christ. The difference in degree becomes a difference in kind, since no other resurrection in Scripture conquers death itself rather than merely delaying it.

typology.type: The anointed King whose horn God exalts
typology.fulfillment: The song's last line names an anointed king who did not yet exist and whose horn, whose strength and honor, God would exalt. David is anointed within a generation of this song and receives an everlasting dynastic promise, yet David's own horn is eventually broken in exile. Jesus receives the title outright, the Christ, God's Anointed, and is exalted not merely to an earthly throne but, in Acts 2:33 and Philippians 2:9, to the right hand of God, given the name above every name; the horn that Hannah could only foresee is finally raised beyond any reach of falling.

typology.type: The Rock beside whom there is no other
typology.fulfillment: Hannah confesses there is no Rock like our God, a title for the LORD's utter uniqueness and steadiness. Paul later identifies that very Rock with the Christ who accompanied Israel in the wilderness, for they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4. What Hannah sang as a name for the one true God, the New Testament applies directly to the Son, so that the unshakable foundation she praised is revealed to have always included the One who would come as Messiah, Himself called the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:20.

study.christ: Zechariah's own prophecy at the birth of John the Baptist borrows Hannah's rarest image outright: he blesses God who has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, Luke 1:69, taking the very word Hannah sang over her own small deliverance and applying it to the coming of Jesus. What Hannah could only voice as hope, that God would one day exalt the horn of His anointed, Zechariah announces as accomplished fact standing at the door of the incarnation. The closing claim that the LORD will judge the ends of the earth also finds its answer in the New Testament's teaching that judgment itself has been handed to Christ: the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22, so the very verdict Hannah expected the LORD Himself to render is now exercised by Jesus as the LORD's own prerogative made visible. Hannah's confession that by Him actions are weighed anticipates a final accounting before Christ's judgment seat, where everyone will appear to give account, 2 Corinthians 5:10, so that her warning against boasting becomes gospel realism about a coming day none can escape by strength or wealth. Even her opening claim that there is no one holy like the LORD is picked up in the song of Moses and of the Lamb in Revelation 15:4, sung by those who had conquered the beast, who ask who will not fear and glorify God's name, since He alone is holy, applying to the enthroned Lamb the very uniqueness Hannah reserved for God. The whole song, then, is not simply background to a single messianic title at its end; every clause reaches toward Christ, His birth announced with her own image of a raised horn, His judgment identified with the LORD's judgment of the earth, His holiness confessed in the same terms as the Father's. Hannah sang before there was any king to sing about; the church sings the same song now knowing His name.
study.god: This song is quietly polemical. In the world around Israel, fertility, harvest and the birth of children were widely credited to a pantheon of fertility deities, Baal and Asherah chief among them, whose favor people sought through ritual across the ancient Near East. Hannah's song grants none of that ground: it is the LORD who opens the womb of the barren and closes that of the fruitful, the LORD who sends both poverty and wealth, the LORD who brings death and gives life. There is no other power at work in the world Hannah describes, and no rival deity gets so much as a mention to be denied; the song simply assumes there is nothing else to reckon with beside the LORD. That total, unshared sovereignty extends even into what looks like sheer chance or bad luck, the failure of a harvest, the loss of a fortune, the empty years of a marriage; the song insists none of it floats free of God's hand, however painful or unjust it may feel from underneath. This raises the hardest question a careful reader can ask of the passage: if God sends poverty as well as wealth, kills as well as makes alive, is He arbitrary or cruel? The song answers by holding sovereignty and goodness together rather than choosing between them, since the same God who brings down also lifts up, and the direction of His power consistently favors the humbled rather than the proud, the barren rather than the fertile, the poor rather than the rich. His rule is not indifferent; it has a moral grain running through it toward mercy for the lowly. The picture of God guarding the very feet of His faithful ones, verse 9, pictures a providence detailed enough to reach the ordinary business of walking through the world, not merely the grand reversals of empires; the God who topples kings also keeps an old woman's steps from stumbling on the path. And His voice, thundering from heaven against His adversaries, verse 10, reminds the reader that intimacy with this God, guarding the steps of the humble, never collapses into a manageable, domesticated deity; the same LORD who bends low to a barren woman's prayer remains the God before whom the proud will one day be shattered.

crossReferences.note: Moses' song already confesses, I bring death and I give life; Hannah sings a closely matching claim in verse 6, showing that her praise is not new theology but the oldest confession of Torah applied to her own answered prayer, tying the barren woman's rescue to the God who spoke through Moses at the founding of the nation.

David's own closing song asks, who is the Rock except our God, echoing Hannah's confession closely. Her prayer at the beginning of the book of Samuel and David's near the very end form a frame around the entire narrative of the rise of the monarchy, both anchored in the same confession of God's unrivaled steadiness.

The psalm lifts the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap and gives the barren woman a home as a joyful mother of children, reproducing Hannah's verse 8 almost exactly; Israel's worship kept singing her song long after her own lifetime, using it as the pattern for praising God's care for the lowest.

God promises to cut off the horns of the wicked while the horns of the righteous are exalted, extending the very image with which Hannah opens and closes her prayer; the horn that marks Hannah's own restored strength becomes an ongoing biblical picture of God's verdict on the proud and the humble alike.

Mary's Magnificat reproduces Hannah's structure and often her very words, praising the God who scatters the proud, fills the hungry, and sends the rich away empty; the pattern of praise Hannah began over the birth of a prophet is renewed over the birth of the Lord Himself.

Zechariah blesses God who has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David, taking Hannah's rarest image, the exalted horn, and applying it directly to the coming of Christ at the very threshold of the New Testament.

Paul names the Rock that followed Israel in the wilderness as Christ Himself; what Hannah confessed as a title for the one true God, the apostle applies directly to the Son, showing her Rock to have always included the One who would come as Messiah.

Christ humbled Himself to death on a cross, and God highly exalted Him, the very shape of Hannah's God who brings down to Sheol and raises up, now embodied in a single, unrepeatable act that secures salvation rather than merely illustrating a pattern.

Peter preaches that this Jesus, crucified, God raised up and exalted to His right hand, making Him both Lord and Christ, the anointed King whose horn Hannah foresaw being lifted beyond the reach of every enemy, fulfilled publicly before the whole house of Israel.

The Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, so the verdict Hannah expected the LORD to render over the ends of the earth is now entrusted to Christ, whose exalted horn is also His authority to judge the world in righteousness.

study.oneStory: Hannah's prayer opens with a claim that reaches back to the very beginning: the foundations of the earth are the LORD's, and He has set the world upon them, so her song of reversal is grounded in the doctrine of creation itself, not merely in one family's luck. The proud boasting she rebukes in verse 3 echoes the primal sin of wanting to be self-sufficient, to secure one's own strength apart from God, the same reach for autonomy that fractured Eden; her song answers that ancient pride with the news that every boast will be humbled and every claim to self-made strength broken like the bows of the mighty. Within Israel's unfolding story, her prayer sits at the exact hinge between the chaos of the judges, when there was no king, and the coming of the monarchy her final words anticipate; the LORD will give power to His king before Israel has ever asked for one, so that when the people later demand a king for the wrong reasons, chapter 8, the reader already knows that the true king was always going to be God's own gift, not a concession to human impatience. The generations of kings that follow, Saul falling, David rising, Solomon's glory and the long slide into exile, all play out under the pattern this song announces at the very start, that the LORD humbles and the LORD exalts according to His own purposes and timing. When the New Testament identifies Jesus as the horn of salvation raised up in the house of David, the long middle of the story, all those centuries of kings who could not keep their own throne, is folded into the single, sufficient reign of the Anointed One Hannah foresaw. And the song's closing hope, that the LORD will judge the ends of the earth, is not resolved until the last pages of Scripture announce that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, who will reign forever and ever, Revelation 11:15, the horn exalted at last beyond every possibility of breaking.

quiz.q: What is Hannah's song mainly about?

options.text: The character of God, who humbles the proud and exalts the lowly, and who will exalt His anointed King.
options.note: The song moves from Hannah's rescue to the God of reversal and His coming Messiah.

options.text: Her thankfulness that God gave her a baby son.
options.note: That is the occasion, but the song's real subject is the God who gave him and the reversal He works.

options.text: A set of promises that faithful people will always become wealthy.
options.note: It celebrates God's reversals, not a guarantee of riches; that misreads the poetry.

options.text: A complaint against God for her years of barrenness.
options.note: The song is joyful praise, not complaint.

quiz.q: Why is it striking that Hannah sings about the LORD's king and anointed?

options.text: Israel had no king yet, so her song functions as prophecy pointing to the coming Messiah.
options.note: The royal climax sets the messianic hope at the door of the book before any king exists.

options.text: It anticipates the monarchy God is about to establish through Samuel.
options.note: True, but understates that the line reaches beyond Saul and David to the true Anointed One.

options.text: It shows Hannah wanted her own son Samuel to become king.
options.note: Samuel was a prophet and judge, not king; the anointed one points elsewhere.

options.text: It proves the song was written long after and has no prophetic weight.
options.note: The passage presents it as genuine, forward-looking praise, not a mere later insertion.

quiz.q: How does Hannah's song connect to the New Testament?

options.text: Mary's Magnificat echoes it, and its anointed King is fulfilled in Jesus the Christ.
options.note: Luke 1 models Mary's song on Hannah's, and the Messiah is the Anointed One she foresees.

options.text: It is echoed by another woman's song at the announcement of a God-given son.
options.note: True of Mary, but this leaves out the fulfillment of the anointed King in Christ.

options.text: It is quoted by Jesus to describe the end of the world.
options.note: There is no such quotation; the link is the reversal theme and the Messiah.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament at all.
options.note: The Magnificat and the messianic hope tie it closely to the gospel.

quiz.q: What does the song teach about God's sovereignty?

options.text: He rules over life and death, wealth and poverty, and uses that power to humble the proud and lift the lowly.
options.note: Verses 6 to 8 join God's total sovereignty to His moral purpose of reversal.

options.text: He is able to raise the poor and bring down the mighty.
options.note: True, but omits the sweep of His rule over life, death, and the earth's foundations.

options.text: He controls only the outcomes of battles between armies.
options.note: His sovereignty here reaches far wider than warfare, over life and death itself.

options.text: He leaves the fortunes of people entirely to chance.
options.note: The song insists the LORD Himself sends poverty and wealth, and humbles and exalts.

quiz.q: Why does Hannah call God the Rock?

options.text: Because in a world of toppling powers and shifting fortunes, He alone is the unshakable, holy foundation.
options.note: The Rock names God as steady refuge amid the reversals she sings, echoing Deuteronomy 32.

options.text: Because God is stronger than her enemies who taunted her.
options.note: True in part, but the title means far more than strength against foes; it means unshakable steadiness.

options.text: Because rocks were used to build the sanctuary at Shiloh.
options.note: The title is a picture of God's steadfast nature, not a reference to building materials.

options.text: Because God is cold and unfeeling toward His people.
options.note: The Rock speaks of steadfast refuge and care, not coldness.

questions: Hannah's answered prayer overflowed into worship that was all about God, not just His gift. When God answers you, do you praise the Giver more than the gift?
The song celebrates a God who lifts the lowly and humbles the proud. Where in your life do you need to stop trusting your own strength, by which no man prevails, and rest on the Rock?
Hannah rejoiced in God's salvation before she could see the whole story. How can her confidence in God's reversals steady you while you wait in a hard or unresolved season?
The song ends by looking ahead to God's anointed King. How does it change your worship to know that Jesus is that Messiah, exalted to judge the earth and to save His people?
Mary later sang almost the same song. What would it look like for your prayers of thanksgiving to be as full of God's character and purposes as Hannah's was?

translationNotes.note: Horn renders qeren, an image of strength and dignity; the BSB footnote allows strength, and the same word returns in verse 10 of the anointed one.
Rock, tsur, is a title for God as unshakable refuge, drawn from the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32.
Anointed renders mashiach, messiah; sung before Israel had any king, it points ahead through David to Jesus the Christ.
